<reason>CON built a sharper, more coherent case by turning PRO's own mechanism against it: PRO needs community cooperation for the "intelligence" that justifies operations, yet CON showed that suspicionless zone searches poison exactly that cooperation, and did so with concrete, plausible actors (shopkeepers, parents, youth workers). CON's central "trilemma" — intelligence precise enough to authorize a search is precise enough to generate individualized suspicion under existing law, and intelligence too vague for that is too vague to search anyone fairly — was introduced in Rebuttal 1, pressed through Pressure Questions, and never squarely dismantled by PRO, who mostly reasserted that a "gap" exists between knowing danger and knowing identity without explaining why that gap justifies searching bystanders with zero individual indicators. PRO's safeguard framework (recorded grounds, independent review, revocation) was a reasonable regulatory answer but CON's timing argument — that trust collapses the moment the rule is announced, while revocation only fires after cumulative harm is already measured — went essentially unanswered in PRO's closing, which repeated the "uncertainty about identity vs. danger" framing without resolving the harm-timing asymmetry. CON's closing crystallized this unresolved clash cleanly, while PRO's closing mostly restated earlier assertions. PRO's opening was clipped for length, a minor execution cost, but the core of CON's case survived intact regardless.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 1 trilemma ([B2.5], later crystallized in [B4.4]/[B5.3]): intelligence sharp enough to authorize a zone search is intelligence current law already permits officers to act on via reasonable suspicion, and intelligence too vague for that is too vague to search anyone fairly — a point PRO never fully escaped despite direct pressure questions targeting it.</best_rebuttal>
